title: What Is Hedging?
subtitle: Using derivatives to reduce risk, not to earn extra profit
openingQuestion: An airline buys oil futures to lock in fuel prices for the next 12 months. Is this speculation?
openingOptions: Yes, because every derivative transaction is speculation
Yes, because they are predicting the price of oil
It's only speculation if it turns a profit
No - this is hedging: they already had a risk from their real business (they must buy real fuel), the derivative just reduces that existing risk, it doesn't create a new one
explanation: Hedging is using derivatives to reduce or eliminate a risk that already exists in a real business operation. The airline is CERTAIN to buy fuel - they just don't know the price. Futures help fix that cost in advance, reducing uncertainty, not creating new risk to chase profit.

diagram.label: Use a derivative to offset that risk

realWorldExample.description: Southwest Airlines was famous for its aggressive oil-price hedging strategy in the 2000s, helping the airline maintain a significant cost advantage over rivals when oil prices surged.

quiz.question: What is the condition for a derivative transaction to be considered pure hedging?
options: It must be approved in writing and formally signed off by the board of directors
There must be a real exposure and a position taken opposite to it
The derivative contract must show a positive net gain
It must use an instrument listed on an exchange
quiz.explanation: The core of hedging is having an existing exposure (risk), and taking a derivative position going in the OPPOSITE direction to that exposure to cancel it out. Trading a derivative to profit from price movement without an underlying exposure is speculation, not hedging.

quiz.question: A Vietnamese exporter signs a sales contract in USD, to be paid in 3 months. Should they hedge 100% of the contract's value with a forward, or leave part of it unhedged?
options: They shouldn't hedge at all since the VND exchange rate has been fairly stable lately
They should only hedge when they forecast the rate will move against them
The hedge ratio is a strategic choice, there is no single correct number
They must hedge exactly 100% of the export contract's value
quiz.explanation: Deciding the hedge ratio is a strategic choice, not a fixed formula - it depends on risk tolerance, how important accurate cash-flow prediction is, and management's view on the future direction of the exchange rate.

quiz.question: An airline locks in oil at 80 USD/barrel, then the price falls to 60. What is the actual economic outcome?
options: The real cost is 70 USD, the average of the two prices
The real cost is 60 USD because they buy at market price
The real cost is 100 USD, the contract's loss added on top
The real cost is still exactly 80 USD, exactly as the hedge intended
quiz.explanation: The physical purchase costs 60, the contract loses 20, the total is still 80 - exactly the locked-in level. But the report only clearly shows the 20 loss, while the certainty gained doesn't appear on any line.

quiz.question: Why doesn't a loss on a hedge contract mean the hedge was wrong?
options: Because hedging is trading the upside for eliminating the downside
Because a hedging loss is booked as a financial expense
Because a hedge only works over many years long-term
Because derivatives transaction fees are usually quite high for smaller firms to absorb
quiz.explanation: A true hedge means giving up the favorable side to eliminate the unfavorable one. Management ending a hedging program after one loss-making year is often exactly the moment the risk returns at the worst time.

quiz.question: What is basis risk in hedging?
options: The risk that the base price swings more than initially expected
The risk that the hedging asset doesn't exactly match the real risk
The risk of insufficient margin when the market moves unfavorably
The risk the counterparty fails to fulfill the contract
quiz.explanation: An airline uses crude oil futures to hedge jet fuel - the two prices move together but not perfectly in step. The remaining gap is the risk left over after hedging.

keyTakeaways: Hedging: reduces an existing risk, doesn't create a new one
Condition: there must be a real underlying exposure to protect
The goal is stability and predictability, not maximizing profit

practicePrompt.question: A Vietnamese exporter has a receivable of 1 million USD due in 3 months, worried about an unfavorable USD/VND move, so signs a forward contract to lock in the exchange rate in advance. What is the purpose of this derivative transaction?
options: The purpose is speculation to earn extra profit from exchange-rate movement over the next 3 months
Hedging reduces an existing risk from the receivable, it doesn't create a new one
The purpose is to increase financial leverage to amplify the company's potential return
This forward contract has no clear purpose, it is just an ordinary administrative procedure
practicePrompt.explanation: Hedging: reduces an existing risk, doesn't create a new one. Unlike speculation (betting to profit), hedging only aims to eliminate the uncertainty from a risk already existing in the business - the company retains that same risk if it doesn't hedge, hedging doesn't add to it.

summary.keyIdea: Hedging: reduces an existing risk, doesn't create a new one
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Condition: there must be a real underlying exposure to protect

application.title: Find a real hedging situation
application.message: Think of a financial risk you or your family actually bear (e.g. a floating-rate loan, or income in foreign currency) and describe an instrument that could help fix that uncertainty.
application.secondary: Hedging only makes sense when there is a genuine underlying risk to protect.

sections.text: Hedging is using derivatives to reduce or eliminate a risk that already exists in a real business operation - not to earn extra profit. The core condition: there must be an underlying exposure (an existing risk) that the derivative position takes an opposite direction to, to cancel it out.
Airlines: certain to buy oil, just not sure at what price

An airline is CERTAIN it must buy fuel to fly - it just doesn't know the price at the actual time of purchase. Futures help fix that cost in advance, reducing uncertainty. Southwest Airlines was famous for its aggressive oil-price hedging strategy in the 2000s, helping the airline maintain a significant cost advantage over rivals when oil prices surged. This is pure hedging: an existing exposure (the need to buy oil), and a futures position that offsets exactly that risk.

A Vietnamese exporter receiving USD payment in 3 months isn't required to hedge 100% of the contract's value with a forward. Hedging 100% removes all uncertainty but also completely gives up any chance to benefit from a favorable rate move. Many companies choose to hedge only part - for example 50-70% - to balance safety and flexibility. This is a strategic choice, not a fixed formula.

sections.title: Why a successful hedge often looks like a loss
sections.equation: Actual cost = Market purchase price ± Gain/loss on the derivative contract

variables.name: The price that must be paid at the time of actual purchase
The result of the hedge position
variables.description: Always opposite in direction to the market price's movement

example.title: An airline locks in the price of oil at 80 USD/barrel via futures for 1 million barrels
example.calculation: Oil price falls to 60 USD → actual purchase costs USD 60 million, but the futures lose USD 20 million · Total: 60 + 20 = USD 80 million
example.result: USD 80 million - exactly the level locked in
example.explanation: If oil rises to 100, the result is still 80 million. That is the entire point. But the report will show a very visible USD 20 million futures loss, while the USD 20 million saved doesn't appear on any line.

sections.label: The most dangerous misunderstanding
sections.text: Treating a loss on a hedge contract as proof the hedge was wrong. A true hedge means giving up the favorable side to eliminate the unfavorable one - it will lose money in roughly half the years, and that is a sign it is running correctly. Management ending a hedging program after one loss-making year is often exactly the moment the risk returns at the worst time.

items: Condition for pure hedging: there must be a real underlying exposure to protect
Goal: stability and predictability, not maximizing profit
The hedge ratio (0-100%) is a strategic decision based on risk tolerance
Trading a derivative to profit from price movement with no underlying exposure - that is speculation, not hedging
